items.item: a point-in-time join reproduces the state of features at a specific point in the past, not their current value
the join scans backward from the entity dataframe's own timestamp up to a maximum of the TTL
the TTL is relative to each entity row's own timestamp, never to the time the query runs
a row older than the earliest feature data, or further from a feature row than the TTL allows, joins to nothing

sources.source: Feature leakage in ML: Detect, Prevent, and Fix It (Hex)

items.item: a post-outcome field is only knowable, or only populated, after the outcome has occurred
the causal test: would this feature's value be known at the exact moment of prediction

An as-of join and a 'snapshot the table periodically' mitigation (Rule #31's own suggestion) solve the same problem to different degrees — a periodic snapshot only gets you 'reasonably close,' in the source's own words, while an as-of join keyed to the label's exact timestamp is exact by construction.

Temporal leakage and post-outcome leakage are easy to conflate because both get called 'leakage,' but they fail differently: temporal leakage is fixed by changing *when* you look (the as-of join), while post-outcome leakage has no 'when' that works, because the field is unpopulated at every moment before the outcome.

A feature TTL and an as-of join are the same mechanism with one extra stop condition: both scan backward from the label's own timestamp, and a TTL simply refuses to accept an answer past a stated distance back, converting 'stale' from an invisible property of the data into an explicit, checkable one.

The naive-join AUC isn't 'wrong data' in the way a bug usually is — every number in it is real and correctly computed from the table as it stood; the bug is purely that the live model will never have access to that same table state at serving time, which is why the gap only ever shows up after shipping, never in an offline test that doesn't also change what it's allowed to see.

Reusing the exact online transformation for a backfill (Rule #32) isn't a style preference — a warehouse-table approximation of 'the same' feature can be correlated with the true online value without ever being equal to it, which is precisely the gap that produces skew without any join-timing bug at all.

items.item: This topic's own examples.py trains the identical simple classifier on both the naive and as-of training sets specifically so the measured AUC gap reflects the join alone, not a confound from comparing two different models.

Choosing batch versus streaming feature computation doesn't change what the as-of join does — it changes only how fresh the feature's as-of value can be relative to when the event that produced it actually happened, which is a separate axis from correctness.

The two TTL edge cases (too early, too stale) both resolve to the same answer — null — for different reasons: one has no feature history yet to scan back into, the other has history that exists but sits outside the stated staleness contract; conflating them as 'missing data' in general loses the distinction between 'never known' and 'known too long ago to trust.'

A naive join's inflated AUC and a post-outcome field's near-perfect correlation with the label look like the same symptom (suspiciously good offline performance) but demand different fixes: the naive join is repaired by changing the join's timing, while the post-outcome field has to be dropped outright, because no timing choice makes an unpopulated-until-after field available earlier.

This topic's own churn scenario deliberately engineers the leakage into a synthetic dataset with a stated random seed, rather than claiming a real company's numbers, so the measured AUC gap is reproducible evidence of the join's effect and not an anecdote borrowed from elsewhere.
